topic: Hot vs cold composting at home

facts.fact: hot piles reach 55-65°C, which kills weed seeds
cold composting takes about 6-12 months or more

search_results.title: Compost basics: browns and greens
search_results.snippet: Compost needs two kinds of material. Browns are dry, carbon-rich things like dead leaves, straw and cardboard. Greens are moist, nitrogen-rich things like vegetable scraps, coffee grounds and grass clippings.

search_results.title: Getting the mix right
search_results.snippet: Microbes work fastest at a carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of roughly 30:1. In practice that is about two to three buckets of browns for every bucket of greens. Too many greens smell; too many browns barely break down.

search_results.title: Hot composting in 4-8 weeks
search_results.snippet: A hot pile needs to be at least about one cubic metre so it can hold heat. Kept damp and turned every few days, it reaches 55-65°C in the centre. That heat speeds decomposition and kills most weed seeds and plant pathogens.

search_results.title: Why turning matters
search_results.snippet: The microbes in a hot pile use oxygen quickly. Turning the pile with a fork mixes the outside into the middle and lets air back in; without it the centre goes anaerobic and starts to smell.

search_results.title: Cold composting: the lazy method
search_results.snippet: Cold composting means adding scraps as you get them and leaving the heap mostly alone. It takes much less work but often needs 6 to 12 months, sometimes longer, and it will not reliably kill weed seeds, so keep seeding weeds out.

search_results.title: How to tell compost is ready
search_results.snippet: Finished compost is dark, crumbly and smells earthy. You should not recognise the original scraps. Screening out lumps and putting them back in the next batch is common.
